notes.title: Start here: five C# sectors inside a React app
notes.body:
Despite its name, `buildsql` is a React app (IPSKILL) that hosts a lesson archive. This quest uses its .NET volume: the five sector lessons under `content-src/vol3/parts/01` to `05`, one `readme.md` each.

1. `01`: the garbage collector, generations and allocation.
2. `02`: choosing collections with numbers.
3. `03`: `IDisposable`, `IAsyncDisposable` and cleanup order.
4. `04`: designing, throwing and filtering exceptions.
5. `05`: System.Text.Json options, converters and contract versioning.

Every readme has the same shape: a model, worked examples, a **Common mistakes** list, an **Interview answer** and a **Check yourself** list of about fourteen questions. The quiz draws mostly from the worked examples and the mistakes lists. A good way to prepare is to answer each Check yourself question in writing before looking anything up, then find the paragraph that settles it.

The lessons are dense and mostly accurate, but a few sentences overstate or date quickly. When something matters, check it against the official .NET documentation.

excerpts.quote: **This is IPSKILL, a React app.** It displays a SQL/TS/Node/React/C#/.NET lesson archive;

notes.title: Concept: where values live and what containers promise
notes.body:
Sectors 1 and 2 are about memory you cannot see in the source code.

**Heap and stack.** A reference-type object always lives on the managed heap. A value type lives wherever its container puts it, and the interesting cases are the containers. Read the bullet in sector 1's Common mistakes that starts with structs and list each container it names.

**Measuring.** Sector 1 shows three ways to count. For each, note what is counted and whether the counter for one generation can move without the others.

**Pools.** `ArrayPool<T>` hands out arrays that someone else may have used. Read the three renting rules and ask what `Rent` promises about the length.

**Collections under pressure.** In sector 2, read the GetOrAdd worked example and note what problem its fix addresses. Then read the mistakes list for what it says about enumeration order.

excerpts.quote: "Which collection should I use?" is asked constantly and answered badly, because the usual answer is a complexity table and the usual reality is a constant factor.

readMore.why: The structure table: what each collection is underneath.

notes.title: Concept: cleanup, failure and wire contracts
notes.body:
Sectors 3 to 5 are about what happens at the edges of a method.

**Cleanup.** A `using` is compiled into a `try`/`finally`. Practise rewriting a `using` by hand as that `try`/`finally`. Also read what sector 3 says about types that implement only `IAsyncDisposable`.

**Async exceptions.** An `async` method is rewritten by the compiler into a state machine, and the method returns a `Task` that records how the body ended. Ask where an exception thrown in the body goes, whether it is thrown before or after the first `await`, and what `await` does with a task that holds several failures. Sector 4's mistakes list covers both.

**Filters.** Read the filter section and pay attention to when a `when` clause runs relative to stack unwinding.

**JSON.** In sector 5, read the options section, look up in the .NET docs which settings `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web` turns on and what a plain `new JsonSerializerOptions()` uses instead, and read the versioning rules for `required`.

excerpts.quote: The one-line version: **an exception is an API**, and it should be designed like one

notes.title: Why a gen2 collection also bumps the gen0 count
notes.body:
Collections are generational and nested: a gen1 collection also collects gen0, and a gen2 collection collects gen1 and gen0 too. The counters reflect that, which is what the guide means by cumulative upward: `GC.CollectionCount(0)` counts every collection that included gen0, which is every collection. So if the gen2 count rose by 1, the gen0 count rose by at least 1.

- The counters are not independent; higher generations include lower ones.
- A gen2 pass does collect gen0, so the count cannot stay the same.
- Counters only increase; promotion does not decrement anything.

excerpts.quote: int gen0 = GC.CollectionCount(0) - g0; // includes gen1 and gen2 passes

notes.title: Why the payload length is yours to track
notes.body:
`Rent(1000)` promises an array of **at least** 1000 elements; pools round up to bucket sizes, so 1024 is normal. The extra 24 bytes are not cleared and may hold data from whoever rented the array before. The guide's example computes its own `taken` length and comments never to use `buffer.Length`. Using 1024 would copy 24 bytes of stale data, or read past the real input.

- `Rent` does not size the array to the request; it may be larger.
- The pool does not zero-fill on rent, and `Return` with `clearArray: false` leaves contents as they are.
- `Return` reports nothing about lengths.

excerpts.quote: `Rent(n)` gives you **at least** n. Track your own length.
int taken = Math.Min(chunkSize, remaining); // NEVER buffer.Length

notes.title: Where a struct in a List<T> lives
notes.body:
`List<T>` stores its items in a `T[]`. For a value type the values are stored inline in that array, and the array is a heap object. So the struct value lives on the heap, inside the list's array, without being boxed. The guide lists this as the first of three ways a struct ends up on the heap.

- The caller's stack frame holds only the argument copy during `Add`; the list keeps its own copy.
- `List<T>` is generic, so no per-element boxing happens; boxing needs a cast to `object` or an interface.
- There is no per-thread pool of struct values.

excerpts.quote: A struct in a `List<T>` lives in the list's array, on the heap.

notes.title: Why GetOrAdd can open several connections
notes.body:
`ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd` does not hold a lock while it runs your value factory. Several threads that miss at the same moment can all run the factory; one result is stored and returned to everyone, and the other values are thrown away. If the factory opens a connection, those extra connections are never closed. The fix in the guide stores a `Lazy<T>` with `ExecutionAndPublication`, so creating the wrapper is cheap and the expensive part runs once.

- No lock is held around the factory, so once is not guaranteed.
- Racing threads do not throw; they get the stored value.
- A key maps to one value; there are never two entries for it.

excerpts.quote: `ConcurrentDictionary` does not hold a lock across your factory, on purpose.

notes.title: Why D shows up where B used to be
notes.body:
`Dictionary` keeps its entries in an array and enumerates that array in index order. Adding A, B and C fills slots 0, 1 and 2. `Remove(B)` does not shift anything; it puts slot 1 on a free list. The next `Add` takes a free slot before appending, so D goes into slot 1, and enumeration gives A, D, C. Order is not part of the contract, which is why the guide warns against relying on it.

- It only looks insertion-ordered until a removal happens.
- New keys are not moved to the front.
- Removal does not compact or reverse the array.

excerpts.quote: It looks insertion-ordered until a removal creates a free slot that the next insert reuses.

notes.title: Why disposal runs in reverse
notes.body:
Each `using var` becomes a `try`/`finally` that wraps the rest of the scope, so the three declarations nest: connection outside, command inside it, reader innermost. Finally blocks run from the inside out, so reader is disposed first, then command, then connection. That order is also the safe one, because each resource depends on the one declared before it.

- Declaration order would close the connection under a live command.
- A connection does not dispose the commands or readers created from it.
- The finalizer thread plays no part; `using` disposes deterministically.

excerpts.quote: Nested `using` blocks are nested `try`/`finally` blocks, so the inner resource is released first.

notes.title: Why a plain using will not compile
notes.body:
A plain `using` statement needs a type convertible to `IDisposable`. A type that implements only `IAsyncDisposable` does not qualify, so the compiler reports an error and suggests `await using`. That is the point of the guide's advice: if release is real I/O, offering only the async interface makes it impossible to call it synchronously by accident.

- The compiler does not call `DisposeAsync` for a plain `using`.
- Nothing compiles, so there is no silent skip at run time.
- No exception is involved; the error is at compile time.

excerpts.quote: If a type genuinely needs async release, make it `IAsyncDisposable` only; the compiler will then stop callers from writing a plain `using`.

notes.title: Where an exception from an async method goes
notes.body:
The compiler turns an `async` method into a state machine, and every exception thrown in its body, even before the first `await`, is caught and stored in the returned task. The call itself returns a faulted task without throwing. The exception is rethrown when someone awaits the task (or reads `.Result`). The guide's fix is a non-async wrapper that validates arguments and then calls the async part.

- No synchronous throw: the task exists and carries the exception.
- The exception is not lost; the task is faulted, not completed.
- Unobserved task exceptions do not crash the process in modern .NET.

excerpts.quote: Argument validation inside an `async` method body, which faults the task instead of throwing synchronously

notes.title: What await throws for a WhenAll with two failures
notes.body:
`Task.WhenAll` returns one task that faults with an `AggregateException` containing every failure. `await` does not throw that aggregate: it rethrows the first inner exception, here t1's. The other failure is still available through the WhenAll task's `Exception.InnerExceptions`, so keep a reference to the task if you need all of them.

- The aggregate itself appears only with `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
- `await` throws once, not once per failure.
- The await waits for all three tasks to finish; it does not need t2 to fail before throwing.

excerpts.quote: `await` unwraps to the first inner exception; the aggregate only appears if you use `.Result` or `.Wait()`.

notes.title: What a false exception filter leaves behind
notes.body:
A `when` filter runs during the first pass of exception handling, before any stack frames unwind. If it returns false, that catch block is simply not chosen and the search for a handler continues. The exception object, and its stack trace, are untouched. That is the difference from catching and then writing `throw;`: by then the stack has unwound to the catch.

- Nothing is caught, so nothing is rethrown or reset.
- A filter is a condition, not a handler; returning false does not swallow anything.
- No wrapping happens; the same exception keeps propagating.

excerpts.quote: the filter is evaluated **before the stack unwinds**, so if it returns false the exception continues untouched — same object, same trace

notes.title: Why plain options miss a camelCase member
notes.body:
A plain `new JsonSerializerOptions()` has no naming policy and matches property names case-sensitively. The JSON member `orderId` therefore does not match the C# property `OrderId`. Unmatched JSON members are skipped by default, so no error is raised and `OrderId` keeps its default of 0. `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web` turns on camelCase naming and case-insensitive reads, which is why the guide says differing options are the usual cause when two services read the same type differently.

- Case-insensitive matching is a Web default, not the default of a plain options object.
- Unknown members are skipped unless you opt into disallowing them, so nothing throws.
- A plain options object has no naming policy; camelCase comes from Web or an explicit setting.

excerpts.quote: `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web` is what ASP.NET Core uses: camelCase, case-insensitive reads, numbers readable from strings.

notes.title: Why required on a v2 member breaks v1 documents
notes.body:
With `required`, System.Text.Json treats a document that lacks the member as invalid and throws a `JsonException`, whatever the member's type. Every document written before v2 lacks the new member, so all of them now fail to deserialize. The guide keeps `required` for members present since v1 and makes later additions nullable or defaulted.

- A missing required member is an error, not a default.
- Extension data captures unknown members, not missing ones.
- Nullability does not relax `required`: the member must still be present.

excerpts.quote: **`required` only for members that existed in v1.** Putting it on a v2 addition rejects every older document.
